title: "one creator, truth is the name"

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ik Onkar, the numeral one that opens the scripture. Your line was one. Did it help, even once, with someone who annoyed you? Day five.

Most of us have a sentence we'd use to introduce ourselves. Name, where you're from, what you do. Now imagine being asked to describe God in a single breath. Not a book. Not a sermon. A few words, short enough to memorize as a child, deep enough to spend a lifetime on. Guru Nanak did exactly that. Right after the symbol for one, at the top of the scripture, comes a short statement Sikhs call the Mool Mantar, the root verse. Children learn it early. Many Sikhs say it every morning. It's only a handful of words in Punjabi, and it holds the whole path the way a seed holds a tree. Today, the first line.
screen: `DESCRIBE GOD IN ONE BREATH.` → `THE ROOT VERSE.` → `A SEED THAT HOLDS A TREE.`

segments.voice: Mool means root. Mantar is a sacred phrase, the Punjabi form of mantra. The root verse. It begins with yesterday's word, Ik Onkar, there is one, and then it says: Sat Naam. Karta Purakh. Take them one at a time. Sat means truth, but it's deeper than true as opposed to false. It comes from an old root meaning what really is, what exists, what lasts. Naam means name. So Sat Naam: truth is the name. Or, as some translate it, the one whose name is truth. The Victorian scholar Max Arthur Macauliffe, who spent years translating Sikh scripture with Sikh scholars beside him, put the opening this way: "There is but one God whose name is true, the Creator." Here's the surprise in naam. On this path the name isn't just a label, the way your name is printed on a bill. Naam comes to mean the whole presence of God, running through everything. So when Sikhs say they remember the name, they mean something like remembering what is real. Then: Karta Purakh. Karta, the doer, the maker. Purakh, the being, the person. The creator. Not a force that set the world going and walked away. The one who is still making. Put the line together and it holds three ideas in five words. There is one. Its name, its nature, is truth. And it creates. Nearly everything else in the scripture unfolds from this. And there's a quiet challenge in it. If truth is the name of God, then telling the truth isn't just manners. It's a way of speaking God's name.
screen: `MOOL MANTAR — THE ROOT VERSE.` · `SAT — WHAT REALLY IS.` · `NAAM — MORE THAN A LABEL.` · `KARTA PURAKH — THE ONE STILL MAKING.` · then, large: `THERE IS BUT ONE GOD WHOSE NAME IS TRUE.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, think of one true thing about your life right now, not the flattering version, just the true one. On the second, sit with it without fixing it. On the third, if you want to, let the words go out with the breath: Sat Naam.
The Mool Mantar, the root verse. Line one: Ik Onkar, Sat Naam, Karta Purakh. There is one, truth is the name, the creator. Fifth word.
Your line: the name is truth. Today, tell one small truth you'd normally smooth over, kindly. Day five.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Mool Mantar at the start of the morning prayer Japji Sahib and at many other times; it stands at the head of the Guru Granth Sahib and is often the first passage children memorize.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: truth (sat) is the name (naam).

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh slogan.
what it means: the first line of the root verse: there is one, truth is the name, the creator.
what a scholar hears: sat comes from an old root meaning being, what really exists. so Sat Naam can be heard as: the name is reality itself.
